newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria to seek debt rating, mulls Eurobond issue.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria to seek debt rating, mulls Eurobond issue.

text.p: Bulgaria's reformist government will seek a new credit rating in September as part of plans to launch a Eurobond issue on global markets next year to help fund huge domestic debt payments, a government official said.

"We will most likely seek a new credit rating from Moody's and Standard & Poor's in September, which will reflect the improved situation in the country from a year ago," government finance adviser George Prohaski told Reuters on Thursday.

The government hopes the new rating will reflect the newly acquired stability in Bulgaria's economy after the introduction next week of an IMF-prescribed restrictive monetary mechanism known as a currency board.
"We will consider placing a Eurobond issue next year after we evaluate what are our funding needs at that time and our servicing capacity over the next years," said Prohaski.
"International investment companies have shown interest in managing the issue," he added.
Borrowing on external markets to service a three trillion lev ($1.8 billion) domestic debt and fund a restrictive budget is an option being considered by the government, which took office last month.
The government has met several investment banks like Goldman Sachs, JP Morgan and SG Warburg to discuss lead arrangement terms, said a government spokeswoman.

The currency board system, designed to restore confidence in the country's weak financial system, bans central bank lending to the government and commercial banks and requires levs in circulation be covered by foreign exchange reserves.
Bulgaria chose the mark as anchor currency and will officially peg the lev at 1,000 to the mark.
Moody's Investors Service assigned a B3 rating in September 1996 to $5 million of Brady Bonds issued in 1994 to restructure an $8.16 billion commercial debt.

Moody's then said the rating reflected the difficulties Bulgaria faced in meeting its foreign obligations and the slow pace of transition to market economy, which in turn, hindered macroeconomic stabilisation.
Bulgaria relied entirely on external lending to meet debt payments last year, which multilaterals were then reluctant to provide due to the country's failure to meet reform targets.
The government's stringent monetary policy, backed by a $510 million standby agreement with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) since March, has led to a noticeable stabilisation.
The lev has traded steady at around 1,600 to the dollar and 950 to the mark in the past three months, after nosediving to 3,000 per dollar in February pressed by political and economic turmoil.

Inflation has since then steadily declined to 5.6 percent in May, minus 0.7 percent in April and 243 percent in February. Interest rates have come down to 1.27 percent monthly from 18 percent in March.
Moody's also assigned last year CAA ratings of foreign currency-denominated long-term bank deposits and Not Prime for ratings of short-term obligations of issuers domiciled in Bulgaria.
"Bulgaria's credibility in the international finance community has much improved since then," said Prohaski.
